para: Several breakthroughs in clean energy have been made over the past decade. In China the S1500 has been developed, this is a 13-story tall zeppelin like craft housing 12 generator units capturing 17MW of energy per year. To put the full 17MW of energy into perspective, that is the equivalent of 25185 UK households for a full year. Moreover, to power all UK households you would need a mere 1135 of these wind turbines. These turbines float between 500 and 10000 meters up, allowing it to operate at altitudes of much higher wind speeds. The report suggests that this breakthrough could “usher in a new age of renewable power generation. Furthermore, it takes far less material cost to implement these turbines for the power generation due to these higher wind speeds and the turbines can be placed much further out at sea than fixed bottom turbines allowing utilisation of 500% of the area that fixed bottom turbines can access according to the Global Wind Energy Council. This is a major breakthrough in green energy technology as the elevated altitudes allows for greater windspeed to be captured and converted into energy.

To name another breakthrough in the sector. Scientist Carvey Ehren Maigue, is in the process of engineering a bioluminescent solar cell which can capture more light than a regular solar panel. This is because bioluminescence converts UV light into visible light meaning that a solar panel with a bioluminescent film over the top can harvest both visible and UV light. Moreover, the film can have light receptors on the sides meaning it can be applied in windows to capture even more energy and be used as if it were a stain glass window (see below).

Seas, oceans, rivers cover 70 percent of our planet providing food, water and energy. Oceans alone make up over 96% of all the water on Earth. It is a well known fact that oceans also are a major contributor to absorbing 30-50% of the CO2 in the environment, a key source of reducing greenhouse gases in the ozone layer. The preservation of our oceans is a vital requirement for a safe and livable Earth.

Though scientists have officially discovered around 240,000 species, it is estimated that the true number of species living underwater could be 2.2 million, almost ten times more than the recorded ocean census. The biggest present threats to life in our oceans are climate change and pollution. Over 8 million metric tons of plastic yearly end up in our oceans killing and endangering millions of animals yearly. It is imperative we work collectively to minimise the impact of plastics in our environment.

Several breakthroughs in clean energy have been made over the past decade. In China the S1500 has been developed, this is a 13-story tall zeppelin-like craft housing 12 generator units each rated at 100kW of energy. This is a grand breakthrough in green energy technology as the elevated altitudes allow for greater windspeed to be captured and converted into energy.
